title: SLO-aware Fill-and-Drain Autoscaler PRD (v0)
summary: Introduce a fill-and-drain autoscaler for Dedicated capacity that prioritizes tenant SLOs during surges by temporarily borrowing from a pooled burst reservoir and draining excess capacity proactively once demand subsides. The controller aims to maximize served demand without violating per-tenant latency SLOs and to provide predictable economic and isolation guarantees.
background: Existing dedicated autoscalers at Redwood either scale by provisioning whole instances or rely on per-tenant soft-burst credits. Customers with latency-sensitive workloads experience tail SLO violations during sudden demand spikes or noisy neighbors. We need an autoscaler that: (a) minimizes cold-start cost, (b) avoids long tail SLO impact by graceful draining, and (c) enforces tenant fairness during simultaneous surges.
problem_statement: How do we let tenants use extra capacity in short bursts while preventing that usage from degrading other tenants' latency SLOs and while giving predictable billing and rollback behavior? Current burst models either allow uncontrolled borrowing (risking noisy neighbor) or are too conservative (causing avoidable failed or throttled requests).
proposal: A central Fill-and-Drain Autoscaler (FDA) that maintains three logical pools: steady-reserve (tenant committed), burst-pool (shared ephemeral credits), and warm-pool (prewarmed instances). On surge, requests are admitted preferentially to steady-reserve; when that saturates, low-latency safe requests can borrow from burst-pool if the projected SLO budget for affected hosts remains positive. When demand falls, FDA begins a draining phase: new burst allocations are cut off and in-flight borrowed work is allowed to finish while requests are gently routed to steady-reserve or throttled. Drain decisions use host-level tail latency signals and model sequence-length-aware cost estimators.
design_principles: 1) SLO-first: never accept allocation that would likely breach a tenant's 99th percentile latency target. 2) Prefer eviction/soft-throttle over preemptive cold eviction. 3) Fair share allocation across tenants proportional to committed tier and recent usage. 4) Predictive smoothing: use short-window forecasting to avoid oscillation. 5) Operational observability: every borrow must emit telemetry and be traceable to a decision reason.
user_stories: As a product engineer for a payments integration, I want spikes to be served without hitting 99p latency violations so checkout flows remain reliable.
As a platform operator, I want predictable tenant billing for burst use and an audit trail of borrow events to resolve disputes.
As a tenant admin, I want the option to opt-out of borrowing or to cap burst spend per billing period.
As an SRE oncall, I want automatic degradation steps that reduce borrow admissions before manual intervention is required.
acceptance_criteria: System admits burst traffic while keeping affected tenants' 99p latency within SLO 95% of the time (measured across 30-day window).
Burst borrowing events include reason codes, host-level latency risk score, and tenant allocation delta and are queryable in Console.
Rollback behavior: when a tenant's SLO risk crosses high threshold, borrow allocations for that tenant are revoked within 30s and requests are routed to safe fallback model variants if configured.
Billing shows clear line-item for burst minutes and has a tenant-level cap enforcement that prevents overspend.
metrics: fraction of requests served from warm-pool
number of borrow revocations and reason codes
telemetry_and_tracing: Span: autoscaler.decision.{allow|deny|revoke} with tags: slo_risk, forecast_confidence, model_variant
Console dashboard: Borrow heatmap by region/tenant + 99p latency overlay
ops_runbook: On high borrow.revocations alert: 1) Check the SLO-risk dashboard and recent host-level tail spikes. 2) If a single tenant shows persistent tail spikes, temporarily disable that tenant's borrow flag and open a support case. 3) If region-wide risk observed, expand warm-pool size or trigger soft-eviction lanes. 4) For billing disputes, export borrow events (timestamped) and cross-check with Console audit entries.
api_and_config_examples:
Example route config (JSON/YAML style):
- route: payments-checkout
  steady_reserve: 8 vGPU-seats
  burst_allowed: true
  burst_cap_monthly_usd: 1500
  burst_priority: 0.8  # 0-1, higher -> more likely to borrow
  slo_target: 99p=250ms
  fallback: [small-model:latency-saver]
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary, 2 weeks): enable FDA for internal tenants and 3 opt-in customers in us-west. Monitor 99p SLO and borrow revocations. Phase 2 (gradual ramp, 4 weeks): open to beta customers in us-east and eu-west with tenant caps. Phase 3 (GA): enable on all Dedicated clusters with UI controls in Console and billing line items. Each phase gated by SLO metrics and oncall readiness.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Incorrect SLO risk scoring causes over-admission -> mitigation: conservative safety multiplier in initial rollout (0.6) and kill-switch if cross-tenant SLO breach observed.
Risk: Billing surprise for customers -> mitigation: default opt-in is false; explicit tenant consent required; Console shows projected monthly cost before enabling.
Risk: Oscillation between warm-pool scaling and borrow allocations -> mitigation: hysteresis windows and forecast smoothing, require 3 consecutive windows before scale-down.
open_questions: What is the canonical algorithm for computing host-level 'slo_risk' that integrates queue length, recent tail latencies, and model sequence length?
How do we set default burst_priority per pricing tier? (should enterprise tenants get priority over free-tier?)
Should borrow events be refundable in disputed cases or handled purely as post-facto billing adjustments?
next_steps: Engineering spike: implement a host-level slo_risk shim and lightweight simulator (2 engineers, 3 weeks).
Create Console mockups for borrow consent and per-tenant projected cost (design, 1 week).
Legal: draft burst billing language for enterprise contracts (commercial counsel, 1 week).
SRE: prepare canary cluster and run chaos tests that inject tail latency to validate revoke behavior (2 weeks).
